**Nigredo**

The gyre has a womb in it, and I am its hour.
The widening dark unspools me like a thread.
I turned the clock's hands backward in the tower
and set the moon to nursing at my head.

My mother's mirror keeps a sliver of my face,
a cold coin paid to something under glass.
I feed it milk. I feed it Latin. In the grate
the ashes rearrange themselves to ask.

I have swallowed the alphabet of falling things —
the sigil, the salt, the seven-knotted cord.
Beneath the floor a small drum practices its wings.
Beneath the drum, the black smell of a word.

Ceremony is a bandage. Innocence, a stain
that will not lift from linen or from lung.
The tower leans. The horses drink the rain.
A patient brightness limbers up its tongue.

I am the oven and the thing inside the oven.
I am the wax, the wick, the small blue crown.
Call it a daughter. Call it the dove. And when
it opens, say the year, then lay you down.

Nothing is finished. The gyre keeps its promise:
one turn more and the glass will hold us all.
Hang the bees' hum in the doorway like a kiss.
Whatever comes, comes crowned — and comes to pull.

---

The scaffolding is Yeats (quatrains, the gyre, tower, ceremonial cadence, apocalyptic future tense); the interior is Plath (the mirror-mother, the oven, bees, the flat declarative sentences that arrive like a knife set down on a table). The slant rhyme is doing the merging work — Yeats's forms holding, Plath's off-rhymes bending them.
